claim: Rat dams conditioned to fear an odor froze when tested alone.
source: Conditioned dams from both age groups froze when exposed to the conditioned peppermint odor alone (immobility levels increased during exposure to the odor for both age groups: PP4-6 from 6.1 ± 3.2% during baseline to 85.7 ± 6% post odor exposure; PP19-20 from 3.5 ± 2.4% during baseline to 80.6 ± 9.3% post odor exposure, See Figure 1 and Video 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of immobility levels before and after odor exposure, with reference to Figure 1 and Video 1.

claim: Rat dams conditioned to fear an odor showed very little freezing behavior when tested in the presence of their pups.
source: Conditioned dams exposed to the peppermint odor in the presence of their pups behaved very differently, showing very little freezing behavior (PP4-6 baseline freezing 0% and freezing during odor exposure 0.7 ± 0.5%; PP19-20 baseline freezing 0.1 ± 0.1% and freezing during odor exposure 0.4 ± 0.2%, Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of freezing behavior with and without pups present, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: There was a significant difference in the increase in freezing upon odor exposure between dams tested alone versus tested with their offspring for both PP4-6 and PP19-21 age groups.
source: When comparing the increase in freezing upon odor exposure across dams tested alone versus tested with their offspring we found a significant difference (PP4-6, n(w)=8 and n(wo)=8, U = 0.0, p=0.000; PP19-21, n(w)=8 and n(wo)=8, U = 0.0, p=0.000; Figure 1C and D top panels).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test) showing p=0.000 for both age groups, with reference to Figure 1C and D.

claim: PP4-6 dams tested with pups spent much of their time pushing bedding towards the tube that delivered the threatening peppermint odor.
source: When tested in the presence of their pups, PP4-6 dams spent much of their time pushing the bedding towards the tube that delivered the threatening peppermint odor.
evidence: Direct observation of maternal behavior during testing.

claim: The behavior of pushing bedding towards the odor source may correspond to defensive burying reported elsewhere.
source: This behavior may correspond to defensive burying reported elsewhere (Blanchard et al., 2005; De Boer and Koolhaas, 2003; Poling et al., 1981).
evidence: Interpretation of observed behavior supported by citations to previous literature on defensive burying.

claim: PP4-6 dams showed increased locomotion suggestive of exploration of the nesting area when tested with pups.
source: PP4-6 dams also showed increased locomotion suggestive of exploration of the nesting area.
evidence: Direct observation of maternal behavior during testing.

claim: PP4-6 dams increased behaviors directed towards the threat from 2.6 ± 1.2% during baseline to 45.2 ± 6% post odor exposure.
source: We categorized these behaviors as responses directed towards the threat: PP4-6 from 2.6 ± 1.2% during baseline to 45.2 ± 6% post odor exposure (Figure 1E and Video 1).
evidence: Quantitative measurements of behaviors categorized as directed towards the threat, with reference to Figure 1E and Video 1.

claim: PP19-21 dams showed very few displays of defense behaviors towards the threat when tested with pups.
source: Dams with the older pups showed very few displays of defense behaviors towards the threat: PP19-21 from 2.2 ± 1% during baseline to 3.6 ± 1.7% post odor exposure (Figure 1F).
evidence: Quantitative measurements of behaviors directed towards the threat in PP19-21 dams, with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: There was a significant difference in the increase in behaviors targeted towards the threat between dams tested alone versus tested with their offspring only for PP4-6 dams.
source: When comparing the increase in behaviors targeted towards the threat across dams tested alone versus tested with their offspring we found a significant difference only for dams of younger pups (PP4-6, n(w)=8 and n(wo)=8, U = 0.0, p=0.000 and PP19-21, n(w)=8 and n(wo)=8, U = 27.5, p=0.645; Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing significant difference for PP4-6 (p=0.000) but not PP19-21 (p=0.645), with reference to Figure 1E and F.

claim: PP19-21 dams spent most of their time in close contact with the pups, either nursing or grooming them, when exposed to the conditioned threat.
source: In contrast, dams of older pups spent most of their time in close contact with the pups, either nursing or grooming them.
evidence: Direct observation of maternal behavior during testing.

claim: PP19-21 dams increased the amount of time spent with their pups upon exposure to the conditioned threat from 23.1 ± 14.3% during baseline to 72.1 ± 5.7% post odor exposure.
source: We quantified the time spent in contact with the pups (towards pups category), and found that these dams increase the amount of time spent with their pups upon exposure to the conditioned threat (from 23.1 ± 14.3% during baseline to 72.1 ± 5.7% post odor exposure, see Figure 1 and Video 1).
evidence: Quantitative measurements of time spent in contact with pups, with reference to Figure 1 and Video 1.

claim: PP4-6 dams did not increase the amount of time spent in contact with pups upon exposure to the conditioned threat.
source: In contrast, dams with the younger pups did not increase the amount of time spent in contact with them (from 0.2 ± 0.2% during baseline to 4.3 ± 3% post odor exposure, See Figure 1G).
evidence: Quantitative measurements of time spent in contact with pups for PP4-6 dams, with reference to Figure 1G.

claim: There was a significant difference in the increase in time spent with pups upon exposure to the peppermint odor between mothers of young and older pups.
source: Comparing the increase in time spent with the pups upon exposure to the peppermint odor reveals a significant difference between mothers of young and older pups (n(w)=8 and n(wo)=8, U = 10.0, p=0.02, Figure 1G).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing significant difference (p=0.02), with reference to Figure 1G.

claim: Dams suppress freezing when in the presence of their pups.
source: These findings clearly demonstrate that dams suppress freezing when in the presence of their pups.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on the experimental data showing reduced freezing in the presence of pups.

claim: PP4-6 dams spent most of the time directing their behavior towards the threat, whereas PP19-21 dams spent most of the time in close contact with the pups.
source: Whereas the PP4-6 dams spent most of the time directing their behavior towards the threat, the PP19-21 dams spent most of the time in close contact with the pups.
evidence: Summary of observed behavioral differences between the two age groups.

claim: Maternal aggression, the amount of time spent nursing, and circulating hormonal levels in the dams, including those of oxytocin, are quite distinct across PP4-6 and PP19-21 stages of pup development.
source: Indeed, maternal aggression, the amount of time spent nursing, and circulating hormonal levels in the dams, including those of oxytocin, are quite distinct across these stages of pup development (Bosch and Neumann, 2012; Bosch, 2013; Cramer et al., 1990; Higuchi et al., 1985; Thiels et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature documenting differences in maternal physiology and behavior across postpartum stages.

claim: Younger pups do not move away from the nest, whereas older pups have a behavioral repertoire associated with impending independent living.
source: In addition, the behavior of the pups is different, younger pups do not move away from the nest, whereas older pups have a behavioral repertoire associated with impending independent living that includes increased time outside the nest, eating solid food, relying less on nursing and expression of some defensive behaviors, including freezing (Thiels et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature on pup developmental changes.

claim: The behavior of PP4-6 dams tested in the presence of older pups (PN19-23) remained unaltered, suggesting that the behavior of the dams is mostly determined by the maternal stage.
source: The behavior of PP4-6 dams tested in the presence of older pups (PN19-23), remained unaltered, i.e. as before they spent most of the time directing their behavior towards the threat (comparison of time sent directing behavior towards threat during the matched age test with mismatched age test: n=10, Z= −0.561, p=0.575; same comparison for behaviors towards pups: Z= −0.533, p=0.594; Figure 2B), suggesting that the behavior of the dams is mostly determined by the maternal stage.
evidence: Statistical analysis showing no significant difference in behavior with mismatched pups (p=0.575 and p=0.594), with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: PP19-21 dams, when tested with younger pups, changed their behavior such that they now targeted their response more towards the threat, decreasing the time spent with the pups, suggesting that in this case, the behavior of the dams was mostly determined by the behavior of the pups.
source: Conversely, PP19-21 dams, when tested with younger pups, changed their behavior such that they now targeted their response more towards the threat, decreasing the time spent with the pups (comparison of behavior during the matched age test with mismatched age test; behaviors towards threat: n=12, Z= −2.845, p=0.004, behaviors towards pups: Z= −2.824, p=0.005; Figure 2C), suggesting that in this case, the behavior of the dams was mostly determined by the behavior of the pups.
evidence: Statistical analysis showing significant differences in behavior with mismatched pups (p=0.004 and p=0.005), with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Maternal aggression is initially determined by the internal state of the mother but progressively becomes more dependent on the presence of the pups.
source: This is in accordance with previous findings showing that maternal aggression is initially determined by the internal state of the mother but progressively becomes more dependent on the presence of the pups (Caughey et al., 2011; de Almeida et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on maternal aggression.

claim: OTA-dams (PP4-6) displayed increased levels of freezing during odor exposure compared to CONT-dams.
source: We first tested PP4-6 dams with PN4-6 pups and found that OTA-dams (n=8), but not CONT-dams (PBS infused n=6, intact n=4), displayed increased levels of freezing during odor exposure (OTA-dams from 5.2 ± 3.0% during baseline to 60 ± 8.2% post odor exposure; CONT-dams from 0% during baseline to 0.1 ± 0.1% post odor exposure; Mann-Whitney-U test comparing change in freezing by OTA and CONT-dams: n(CONT)=10 and n(OTA)=8, U = 0.0, p=0.000; Figure 3).
evidence: Quantitative measurements of freezing behavior with statistical analysis showing significant difference (p=0.000), with reference to Figure 3.

claim: OTA infusion into CeL abolished behaviors targeting the threat in PP4-6 dams.
source: Concomitantly, OTA infusion into CeL abolished behaviors targeting the threat or the pups (Mann-Whitney-U test comparing change in behaviors towards threat displayed by OTA and CONT-dams: n(CONT)=10 and n(OTA)=8, U=0.0, p=0.000; Mann-Whitney-U test comparing change in behaviors towards pups displayed by OTA and CONT-dams: n(CONT)=10 and n(OTA)=8, U=16.0, p=0.034; Figure 3).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing significant differences in behaviors towards threat (p=0.000) and towards pups (p=0.034), with reference to Figure 3.

claim: OTA-dams (PP19-21) displayed increased levels of freezing during odor exposure compared to CONT-dams.
source: Next, we tested PP19-21 dams with PN19-21 pups and again found that OTA-dams (n=7), but not CONT-dams (again data from PBS, n=7 and intact dams n=10 was pooled), displayed increased levels of freezing during odor exposure (OTA-dams from 0.4 ± 0.4% during baseline to 63.4 ± 5.7% post odor exposure; CONT-dams from 0% during baseline to 0% post odor exposure; Mann-Whitney-U test comparing change in freezing by OTA and CONT dams: n(CONT)=17 and n(OTA)=7, U=0.0, p=0.000; Figure 4).
evidence: Quantitative measurements of freezing behavior with statistical analysis showing significant difference (p=0.000), with reference to Figure 4.

claim: PP19-21 dams receiving OTA injections failed to increase the time spent with the pups upon odor exposure.
source: PP19-21 dams receiving OTA injections failed to increase the time spent with the pups upon odor exposure (Mann-Whitney-U test comparing change in behaviors towards pups displayed by OTA and CONT dams: n(CONT)=17 and n(OTA)=7, U = 6.0, p=0.000; Figure 4)
evidence: Statistical analysis showing significant difference (p=0.000), with reference to Figure 4.

claim: CONT-dams (PP19-21) did not target their actions towards the threat.
source: and as CONT-dams did not target their actions towards the threat either (Mann-Whitney-U test comparing change in behaviors towards threat displayed by OTA and CONT dams: n(CONT)=17 and n(OTA)=7, U = 56.0, p=0.852; Figure 4).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing no significant difference (p=0.852), with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Oxytocin in the CeL suppresses freezing, allowing for the expression of pup defense in the presence of a threat.
source: These results suggest that in the presence of a threat, oxytocin in the CeL suppresses freezing, allowing for the expression of pup defense.
evidence: Inference based on the experimental results showing that blocking oxytocin in CeL prevents suppression of freezing.

claim: A previous study disrupting oxytocin signaling in the central amygdala had no effect on maternal behaviors.
source: Even though a previous study disrupting oxytocin signaling in the central amygdala had no effect on maternal behaviors (Lubin et al., 2003), being other brain areas such as the medial preoptic area and the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis crucially implicated in maternal care (Numan, 2006; Tsuneoka et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The medial preoptic area and the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis are crucially implicated in maternal care.
source: being other brain areas such as the medial preoptic area and the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis crucially implicated in maternal care (Numan, 2006; Tsuneoka et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There was no difference in the amount of time unconditioned dams spent with the pups between OTA and CONT groups when exposed to a neutral peppermint odor.
source: We found no difference in the amount of time dams spent with the pups in either group (Mann-Whitney-U test comparing change in behaviors towards pups displayed by OTA and CONT dams: n(CONT)=8 and n(OTA)=10, U=29.5, p=0.360)
evidence: Statistical analysis showing no significant difference (p=0.360).

claim: Blocking oxytocin in the CeL only affects mother-pup interactions if a threat is present.
source: indicating that blocking oxytocin in the CeL only affects mother-pup interactions if a threat is present.
evidence: Inference based on the finding that OTA had no effect on mother-pup interactions in the absence of a conditioned threat.

claim: Young rodents learn to regulate their defensive behaviors through their mothers.
source: It has previously been shown that young rodents learn to regulate their defensive behaviors through their mothers (Magrath et al., 2006; Mateo and Holmes, 1997; Wiedenmayer, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Rat pups learn to avoid an odor to which they were exposed in the presence of a mother that was conditioned to respond to that odor as a threat.
source: Rat pups learn to avoid an odor to which they were exposed in the presence of a mother that was conditioned to respond to that odor as a threat (using a similar paradigm as the one reported here) (Chang and Debiec, 2016; Debiec and Sullivan, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Only the pups of the conditioned CONT-dams learned to freeze to the peppermint odor.
source: We found that only the pups of the conditioned CONT-dams learned to freeze to the peppermint odor (pups of OTA-dams from 1.4 ± 0.3% during baseline to 3.2 ± 0.8% post odor exposure; pups of CONT-dams from 7.4 ± 1.7% during baseline to 20.2 ± 2.8% post odor exposure; Mann-Whitney-U test comparing change in freezing by pups of OTA and CONT dams: n(CONT)=21 and n(OTA)=18, U=52.5, p=0.000; Figure 5).
evidence: Quantitative measurements of pup freezing behavior with statistical analysis showing significant difference (p=0.000), with reference to Figure 5.

claim: Close proximity between mother and pups may be required for pups to show normal learning about the threat.
source: Since OTA-dams spent most of the time freezing, whereas control dams spent more time with the pups during odor exposure, our finding suggests that close proximity between mother and pups may be required for pups to show normal learning about the threat.
evidence: Inference based on the correlation between maternal behavior (proximity to pups) and pup learning outcomes.

claim: A chemical cue might underlie maternal mediated threat learning by pups.
source: This is consistent with a previous study showing that a chemical cue might underlie maternal mediated threat learning by pups (Debiec and Sullivan, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Pups are not learning to freeze to the threat through behavior copying.
source: In addition, these findings suggest that pups are not learning to freeze to the threat through behavior copying.
evidence: Inference based on the finding that pups of OTA-dams (which froze) did not learn to freeze, whereas pups of CONT-dams (which did not freeze) did learn.

claim: Oxytocin in the central amygdala underlies the suppression of maternal freezing required for active defense of pups.
source: The present studies also show that oxytocin in the central amygdala underlies the suppression of maternal freezing required for active defense of pups.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on the experimental findings showing that blocking oxytocin in CeL prevents suppression of freezing.

claim: The central amygdala has been proposed to act as switch from freezing to other defense responses.
source: The central amygdala has been proposed to act as switch from freezing to other defense responses (Gozzi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Oxytocin can specifically suppress freezing without affecting other outputs of the medial sub-nucleus of central amygdala.
source: In addition, a series of elegant studies describe in detail the mechanisms that could constitute such a switch, focusing on the ability of OT to specifically suppress freezing, without affecting other outputs of the medial sub-nucleus of central amygdala (Knobloch et al., 2012; Viviani et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The switch mechanism involving oxytocin in CeL is required for rat dams to defend their pups when both dams and pups are threatened.
source: The present findings show that this switch is required for rat dams to defend their pups when both dams and pups are threatened, revealing a natural circumstance for OT's modulation of CeA function.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Oxytocin is released upon the introduction of a male intruder and acts on several brain areas thereby modulating maternal aggression.
source: In this paradigm, rat dams actively defend their pups from male intruders that pose a threat to the pups but not the mothers. Oxytocin is released upon the introduction of the male acting on several brain areas thereby modulating maternal aggression (Bosch, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Antagonizing OT with OTA microinjection into CeA was shown to increase maternal aggression.
source: Antagonizing OT with OTA microinjection into CeA was shown to increase maternal aggression (Lubin et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In rat dams selectively bred for high anxiety, OTA infusion into the CeA reduces maternal aggression.
source: However, in rat dams selectively bread for high anxiety, OTA infusion into the CeA has the opposite effect, i.e. it reduces maternal aggression (Bosch et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Oxytocin in central amygdala comes online when the mothers perceive a threat to themselves.
source: Together with the present report, these findings raise the possibility that oxytocin in central amygdala comes online when the mothers perceive a threat to themselves.
evidence: Speculation based on integration of current findings with previous literature.

claim: Oxytocin in central amygdala would not necessarily drive maternal defensive behavior, but rather work as a gate, inhibiting self-defensive behaviors such as freezing and allowing expression of maternal defenses such as aggression towards the threat.
source: Oxytocin in this nucleus would not necessarily drive maternal defensive behavior, but rather work as a gate, inhibiting self-defensive behaviors such as freezing and allowing expression of maternal defenses such as aggression towards the threat.
evidence: Interpretation and speculation based on the experimental findings and integration with previous literature.

claim: Self-defense suppression by rat dams allows for mother-pup interactions that are crucial for pups to learn about threats.
source: Lastly, the present study also provides evidence that self-defense suppression by rat dams allows for mother-pup interactions that are crucial for pups to learn about threats, since pups that were exposed to the odor with OTA-injected dams failed to learn to freeze to it.
evidence: Conclusion based on the experimental finding that pups of OTA-dams did not learn to freeze.

claim: Previous studies have shown maternal influence on the behavior of the pups, including learning about threats.
source: Consistent with previous studies showing maternal influence on the behavior of the pups (Perry et al., 2016; Sullivan and Perry, 2015), including learning about threats (Debiec and Sullivan, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The type of defensive response displayed by the mother determines whether fear of the odor is transmitted to the pups.
source: Importantly, in this study, by manipulating oxytocin signaling in the central amygdala of the mothers, we show that the type of defensive response displayed by the mother determines whether fear of the odor is transmitted to the pups.
evidence: Conclusion based on the experimental findings showing differential pup learning depending on maternal behavior.

claim: Pup learning is mediated by exposure to short-range chemical cues from the mother, such as alarm odor, which requires close proximity between the mother and pups for exposure.
source: We hypothesize that pup learning is mediated by exposure to short-range chemical cues from the mother, such as alarm odor, which requires close proximity between the mother and pups for exposure (Chang and Debiec, 2016; Debiec and Sullivan, 2014).
evidence: Hypothesis based on current findings and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The decrease in freezing by mother rats in the presence of offspring is unlikely to be specific to the presence of offspring.
source: Hence, the decrease in freezing by mother rats reported here is unlikely to be specific to the presence of offspring.
evidence: Inference based on comparison with previous studies showing social buffering of fear in other contexts.

claim: Male and female adult rats freeze less to a conditioned cue when in the presence of other male rats.
source: Particularly relevant are the studies showing that male and female adult rats freeze less to a conditioned cue when in the presence of other male rats (Ishii et al., 2016; Kiyokawa et al., 2004, Kiyokawa et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The suppression of self-defense mechanism allows pup protection.
source: Still, this mechanism allows pup protection. Indeed, in our study we show that mother rats do not stay indifferent to the threat, but rather actively direct their behavior towards the threat or the pups.
evidence: Conclusion based on the experimental observations of maternal behavior.

claim: Parental defense is widespread across taxa, including fish, reptiles, birds and mammals.
source: Parental defense is wide spread across taxa, including fish (Carlisle, 1985), reptiles (Greene et al., 2006), birds (Ghalambor and Martin, 2001) and mammals (Blank et al., 2015), strongly suggesting that it has been selected multiple times.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature across different taxa.

claim: Parental defense has been selected multiple times across taxa.
source: Parental defense is wide spread across taxa, including fish (Carlisle, 1985), reptiles (Greene et al., 2006), birds (Ghalambor and Martin, 2001) and mammals (Blank et al., 2015), strongly suggesting that it has been selected multiple times.
evidence: Inference based on the widespread occurrence of parental defense across taxa, supported by citations.

claim: Evidence that rat dams suppress their own defense responses when threatened in the presence of pups is scarce.
source: Evidence that rat dams suppress their own defense responses when threatened in the presence of pups is scarce (Pinel et al., 1990; Sukikara et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to limited previous literature.

claim: The social environment modulates defensive behavior, such as freezing in adult rats.
source: However, it is well described that the social environment modulates defensive behavior, such as freezing in adult rats (Kikusui et al., 2006; Kiyokawa et al., 2004 Knapska et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Rat dams will attack an adult male that poses a danger to the pups but not themselves, whereas virgin females do not.
source: and that rat dams will attack an adult male that poses a danger to the pups but not themselves, whereas virgin females do not (Bosch, 2013; Giovenardi et al., 2000; Knapska et al., 2010; Mayer and Rosenblatt, 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Oxytocin has been implicated in a number of maternal behaviors including nursing, pup retrieval and maternal aggression.
source: Oxytocin (OT), a highly conserved neuropeptide, has been implicated in a number of maternal behaviors including nursing, pup retrieval and maternal aggression (Carter, 2014; Insel et al., 1998; Pedersen et al., 1992)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Oxytocin's role in maternal behaviors involves brain regions such as the medial preoptic area, anteroventral periventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus, auditory cortex and lateral septum among others.
source: involving brain regions such as the medial preoptic area, anteroventral periventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus, auditory cortex and lateral septum among others (Bosch et al., 2004; Leng et al., 2008; Marlin et al., 2015; de Almeida et al., 2014; Scott et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Oxytocin suppresses freezing, a conserved defense response to inescapable threats.
source: In addition, oxytocin suppresses freezing, a conserved defense response to inescapable threats (Bale et al., 2001; Huber et al., 2005; Knobloch et al., 2012; Veenema and Neumann, 2008; Viviani et al., 2011; Windle et al., 1997; Zoicas et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Oxytocinergic neurons from the peri-ventricular hypothalamus (PVN) project to the centro-lateral nucleus of the amygdala (CeL).
source: In rodents, oxytocinergic neurons from the peri-ventricular hypothalamus (PVN) project to the centro-lateral nucleus of the amygdala (CeL) (Knobloch et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The centro-lateral nucleus of the amygdala (CeL) is a brain region that regulates conditioned threat responses.
source: a brain region that regulates conditioned threat responses (Fanselow and Wassum, 2015; Haubensak et al., 2010; Ciocchi et al., 2010; Wilensky et al., 2006; Li et al., 2013; Ciocchi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the CeL, the release of oxytocin excites CeL-off cells thereby inhibiting freezing to a learned threat.
source: In this amygdaloid sub-nucleus the release of oxytocin excites CeL-off cells thereby inhibiting freezing to a learned threat (Bosch and Neumann, 2012; Huber et al., 2005; Knobloch et al., 2012; Viviani et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The natural circumstances under which animals rely on oxytocin's regulation of freezing remains untested.
source: Although the mechanism by which oxytocin regulates freezing is characterized in great detail, the natural circumstances under which animals rely on it remains untested.
evidence: Statement about the gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Oxytocin in the CeL is required for the suppression of freezing in mothers, thereby permitting active protection of their offspring when both mothers and pups are threatened.
source: We hypothesized that oxytocin in the CeL is required for the suppression of freezing in mothers, thereby permitting active protection of their offspring when both mothers and pups are threatened.
evidence: Statement of the hypothesis tested in the study.

claim: Maternal defense is initially determined by maternal stage progressively becoming more dependent on the pups.
source: Furthermore, we found that maternal defense is initially determined by maternal stage progressively becoming more dependent on the pups, a similar pattern to that observed for maternal aggression (Caughey et al., 2011; de Almeida et al., 2014).
evidence: Conclusion based on the experimental findings, supported by citations to previous literature on maternal aggression.

claim: No differences were found between PBS and intact dams in the oxytocin antagonist experiments.
source: In addition, we tested intact dams alongside both PBS and OTA-dams, to assess whether the infusion procedure itself did not disrupt the behavior of dams. As no differences were found between PBS and intact dams, henceforth we report the pooled data from the two groups (CONT-Dams; see Materials and methods section).
evidence: Statement about control experiments showing no effect of the infusion procedure itself.

claim: Rat pups do not learn amygdala-dependent defense behaviors in response to a self-experienced threat, such as shock, before PN10.
source: Importantly, we tested PP19-20 dams with PN19-20 pups, as learning to avoid an odor from the mother was tested with pups at slightly older age (PN6-7) then our young pup group (PN4-6) and rat pups do not learn amygdala-dependent defense behaviors in response to a self-experienced threat, such as shock, before PN10 (Barr et al., 2009; Moriceau et al., 2010; Sullivan et al., 2000; Wiedenmayer and Barr, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on pup developmental neurobiology.

claim: Similar variance in freezing levels was found within and between litters of pups from CONT-dams.
source: Given the variance in the levels of freezing displayed by pups of CONT-dams, we investigated whether these were more similar within than between litters and found similar variance within and between litters (data not shown).
evidence: Statement about additional analysis performed to assess variance in pup freezing behavior.

claim: All behavioral experiments were performed in accordance with NIH guidelines and approved by the Nathan Kline Institute's Institutional Care and Use Committee (Protocol: AP2015-522).
source: All behavioral experiments were performed in accordance with NIH guidelines and approved by the Nathan Kline Institute's Institutional Care and Use Committee (Protocol: AP2015-522).
evidence: Statement about ethical approval and compliance.

claim: Primiparous dams (Long-Evans) were born and bred at the Nathan Kline Institute in Orangeburg, NY.
source: Primiparous dams (Long-Evans) were born and bred at the Nathan Kline Institute in Orangeburg, NY.
evidence: Statement about the source and strain of animals used.

claim: Litters were culled to 12 pups, six females and six males.
source: Dams were carefully monitored, and upon gestation, litters were culled to 12 pups, six females and six males.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure.

claim: Surrogacy is a standard practice in the Sullivan lab, to which neither rat dams nor pups display abnormal behaviors.
source: It should be noted that surrogacy is a standard practice in the Sullivan lab, to which neither rat dams nor pups display abnormal behaviors.
evidence: Statement about standard laboratory practices and their effects.

claim: Maternal behavior in the home cage of both PP4-6 and PP19-21 dams with both matched and mismatched pups were indistinguishable.
source: We examined the maternal behavior in the home cage of both PP4-6 and PP19-21 dams with both matched and mismatched pups, which when compared were indistinguishable.
evidence: Statement about control observations of maternal behavior.
